title: Eight Weeks Toward Being the Dad You Never Had
subtitle: An eight week plan from James Bell for anyone raised without a father, or by one who hurt them. Grief, God as Father, older men to watch, going back when you fail, and a blessing to pass on.
intro:
This is an eight week walk for the man who is raising children, or soon will be, without ever having watched a father do it. Your father may have left, or never come at all, or died before you knew him, or stayed and made the house a frightening place. Each week holds one focus, one small daily practice, one thing to read, one tool to use, and one honest question. It moves slowly on purpose, from naming the absence and the fear of repeating it, through grief and the hard word Father, to the older men you can learn from, the patterns that rise under pressure, going back to your children when you fail, and the blessing you can give them even if you never heard one. I was raised without a father, and I have five sons. If you're a woman raised without a father, or a mother raising children without theirs, much of this is yours as well, and the care page has a word written for you.

It isn't a cure, and it isn't a substitute for a doctor, a licensed counselor, a pastor, or the real people who can walk with you. If your father, or anyone, could still hurt you or your children, start with safety: the Find Help page lists the hotlines, and in an emergency, call 911. If your own anger has already frightened someone at home, don't wait for week five; call a counselor now. Walk the plan imperfectly. A missed week is not failure; you just pick it back up. Fathering is learned over years, mostly by going back, and these weeks work the same way.
careNote: If your anger has frightened anyone at home, or memories of your father return with panic or nightmares, see a licensed counselor; if you're drinking to cope, talk to your doctor before you try to stop. Find Help lists the Domestic Violence Hotline and SAMHSA's helpline; in an emergency, call 911, and in a crisis, call or text 988.

weeks.focus: Naming the absence and the fear
weeks.why: The gap tends to surface at odd hours. You're walking the floor with a newborn at two in the morning, and it comes to you that no one ever showed you how a man does this. Or you're standing over a son who lied to you, and a voice comes out of you that you swore you'd never use. Many men raised this way carry a private vow never to be like their fathers, and a quieter fear that the vow won't hold. Left vague, the fear only grows. Through Ezekiel, God answered people who claimed they were paying for their fathers' sins, and he described a son who "sees all the sins his father has committed, considers them, and does not do likewise" (Ezekiel 18:14). Before that son chose differently, he looked hard at what his father had done, and that is where this week begins.
weeks.practice: Each day, write down one moment you're afraid of repeating: a child who defies you, say, or a night when money is short and you're spent. Beside it, write what your father did, or failed to do, and what you wish he had done. Keep the pages private, and if they stir up more than you can carry, take them to a counselor. By the week's end, circle the one or two you fear most.

read.label: The care page on being a dad when you never had one, with where to start and when to get more help

tool.label: The Find Help page, with the crisis lines in full, the Domestic Violence Hotline among them

weeks.reflection: What am I most afraid of becoming as a father, and how long have I carried that fear without telling anyone?

weeks.why: Under the fear there's usually a grief that never got its turn: the games he didn't come to, the things nobody taught you, the word of pride you never heard. If he died when you were small, there may be no one to blame, only a gap. If he left or hurt you, the grief comes tangled with anger, and both belong in prayer. Psalm 27 bears David's name, and it prays, "Though my father and mother forsake me, the LORD will receive me" (Psalm 27:10). Grieving him isn't excusing him. The command to "Honor your father and mother" (Exodus 20:12) still stands, but honoring a father who abused you never requires contact with him, or putting yourself or your children where he can hurt you. You can honor him by refusing revenge and contempt while you tell the truth and keep your distance.
weeks.practice: Each day, write down one specific thing you didn't get from your father: a birthday he missed, something you had to figure out alone, a word you waited for. Then read Psalm 27:7-10 aloud and tell God what that one thing cost you, anger included. If you're afraid of him, the Domestic Violence Hotline on Find Help can help you plan for safety.

read.label: Difficult Family, on honoring a parent without pretending the harm away, and on keeping your distance where there has been abuse

tool.label: Psalm 27 in the Study Bible, with notes on its setting and a question on the father and mother of verse 10

weeks.reflection: What did I most need from my father that I never got, and have I ever let myself grieve it?

weeks.focus: When Father is a hard word
weeks.why: Beneath the fear sits a word. Long before anyone in a church calls God Father, a child learns at home what the word means, and for many it comes attached to the man who left or the one who made the house afraid. Scripture never asks you to take that man and enlarge him. Through Hosea, God speaks as a parent who taught a child to walk and "bent down to feed them" (Hosea 11:4). In Jesus' story, a father sees his son far off and "ran to his son, embraced him, and kissed him" (Luke 15:20) before the son had said a word. If the word still sticks, start with Shepherd or Rock, and take the years you need. Paul wrote that the Spirit cries "Abba, Father" in our hearts (Galatians 4:6), so on the days you can't pray the word, it is still being prayed in you.
weeks.practice: Each day, read Hosea 11:1-4 or Luke 15:11-24 slowly. Then tell God in one plain sentence what your father was and wasn't. Begin your prayer with Father if you can. If you can't yet, begin with Lord or Shepherd, and end with the Lord's Prayer, letting Jesus' words say what yours can't.

read.label: Fatherhood: A Bible Study for Men Without a Blueprint, session one, on the father wound and the father in Luke 15 who ran

tool.label: Hosea 11 in the Study Bible, where God remembers teaching a child to walk, with notes on its setting

weeks.reflection: When I pray the word Father, what do I picture first, and what would it take to let God be different from that picture?

weeks.why: Most of what a good father knows, he never read in a book. He absorbed it by watching a man for years: how he answered a teenager who slammed a door, what he did when money ran short, how he said sorry to his wife. That's what you missed, and no book fully replaces it, but you can still watch. Paul told the church in Corinth, "you do not have many fathers" (1 Corinthians 4:15), urged them to imitate him, and sent them Timothy, "my beloved and faithful child in the Lord" (1 Corinthians 4:17), a son by faith and not by blood. The church was meant to be a place where men without fathers find older men to watch. We've often sorted people by age instead and left young fathers to guess, so you may have to ask.
weeks.practice: Each day, pray by name for one man a few years further down the road whose children still like being around him. Before the week ends, ask him for one coffee and two or three honest questions: how he handles his anger, how he apologizes to his kids, what he wishes he'd known sooner. If you're a woman, look for an older couple whose home you trust.

read.label: How to Find a Mentor, on asking small: one coffee and one specific thing you want to learn

tool.label: The Parenting Stage Guide, what a child needs at your child's age and the mistakes to avoid, to sharpen your questions

weeks.reflection: Which man do I know whose children still like being near him, and what keeps me from asking him how he does it?

weeks.why: When you're tired or cornered, you reach for whatever you saw growing up, and where you saw nothing, fear fills the gap. For some men it comes as anger that flares far out of proportion to a spilled cup. For others it's withdrawal: the long silence, the closed door, the evening spent anywhere but with the children. Scripture names both. The letter to the Colossians says, "Fathers, do not provoke your children, so they will not become discouraged" (Colossians 3:21). And after Absalom had his half-brother killed, David let him come home but refused to see him for two years (2 Samuel 14:24, 28). He neither faced what had happened nor drew near, and the resentment that grew in the distance ended in revolt. Neither pattern is your fate, and neither breaks under a vow. What loosens them is being seen early and named honestly, again and again.
weeks.practice: Each evening, write one line about when the old pattern rose that day, the heat or the urge to disappear, and what set it off. Pick one move for next time: say you need ten minutes, step out, and come back. If your anger has frightened anyone at home, call a counselor now, not after one more try. If you're ever afraid you might hurt your child, make sure the child is safe, step away, and call someone right then.

read.label: Is Anger a Sin? On the quick fuse and the cold one, the pause before you speak, and what to do when anger has frightened your home

tool.label: 2 Samuel 14 in the Study Bible, where David brings Absalom home and will not see him, with notes on what the distance cost

weeks.reflection: When the pressure rises, do I tend to burn or to disappear, and who in my house pays for it?

weeks.why: Every father fails his children, usually on an ordinary weeknight over something small. The question is what happens next, and many men never once saw a father come back. Jesus told his hearers that if they remembered at the altar that a brother had something against them, they should leave the gift there and "first go and be reconciled" (Matthew 5:24). A child is owed no less. When you go back after yelling or punishing in anger and name what you did without excuses, your child learns that the relationship can hold a wrong, and that grown men repent too. Going back doesn't cancel a fair rule; keep the rule, and apologize for the shouting. Each return lays down a different pattern from the one you were handed. If you've hit or threatened anyone in anger, though, an apology is only a start; get help now.
weeks.practice: Each night this week, ask whether there's anything to go back for. When there is, go once you're calm: name what you did with no but attached, say you're sorry, and ask your child to forgive you, accepting it if they aren't ready. If your children are grown, a letter or a call that names one specific wrong can begin it, and they decide what comes next.

read.label: How to Apologize to Your Kids, on the four parts of a full apology and keeping a right boundary while you repair

tool.label: Parenting Bible Verses, the set for when you fail as a parent, with a short note on repair

weeks.reflection: What have I never gone back to make right with my children, and what am I protecting by leaving it alone?

weeks.why: A man raised without a father may spend years listening for a word he never heard. At the Jordan, before Jesus had preached or healed anyone, a voice came from heaven: "You are My beloved Son; in You I am well pleased" (Mark 1:11). The delight came before the work. That is the shape of a blessing: not a review of what a child has done, but delight in who the child is, spoken aloud. When people brought children to Jesus and the disciples rebuked them for it, he was indignant, and he "took the children in His arms, placed His hands on them, and blessed them" (Mark 10:16). You can give your children a word you never received, because it never started with your father.
weeks.practice: Each night, put a hand on each child's shoulder, if they welcome it, and say one sentence of delight that has nothing to do with how they did that day: I'm glad you're mine, or I love who you're becoming. Add the old words if you like: "May the LORD bless you and keep you" (Numbers 6:24). If your children are grown, write it in a letter.

read.label: How to Bless Your Children, on touch, words of delight, and a good future spoken over a child until it becomes a rhythm

tool.label: The Prayer Planner, give each of your children a day of the week and pray for that child by name

weeks.reflection: What word have I waited my whole life to hear from a father, and which of my children needs to hear it from me this week?

weeks.why: Eight weeks haven't filled the gap, and nothing will entirely; some nights the old pattern will still rise. But the center has moved. The vow never to be like him kept your father in the middle of your life, and now other things stand there: a Father who receives you, men you can watch, children you've gone back to and begun to bless. Psalm 68 calls God "a father of the fatherless" (Psalm 68:5) and says "God settles the lonely in families" (Psalm 68:6), often through his people. So a man who was never fathered is fathered after all, late and by other means, and learns to father by turning toward his children again and again. In time, a younger man may be watching you.
weeks.practice: Write on a card the two or three practices from these weeks that actually helped, such as going back, the nightly blessing, or a standing breakfast with an older man, and when you'll keep each one. Then keep them. Show the card to one man and ask him to check on you in a month. If a younger father is a step behind you, invite him over some Saturday.

weeks.reflection: What do I want my children to carry from me into their own homes, and what am I doing this week to hand it to them?
